title: Madhva hears 'not that'
hookLine: one merged sound lets Madhva's school hear 'you are not that'
carry: for madhva, difference makes devotion possible
tomorrow: 'that' points far away. which word points right here?

cards: Autocorrect swaps one letter, and a whole text flips its meaning. One small sound can do that. Spoken Sanskrit runs its words together: where two a-sounds meet, they melt into one long a, and the seam disappears.
In the Chandogya, the refrain runs: sa atma, tat tvam asi. That is the self; that you are. Said aloud, the seam after atma can't be heard.
Madhva's school hears another word hiding there. Atat. Not that.

teach.b: Madhva, the teacher of the Dvaita school, reads the line as sa atma, atat tvam asi. You are not that. For Madhva, the self and the Lord are really different, and the difference lasts.
It isn't a flaw to get past. In his school, it's what makes devotion possible: one to love, and one who loves. His readers look again at Uddalaka's pictures, too.
The bird on its string comes home to the post it's tied to. The rivers run into the sea. In each, they point out, there's something that depends and something it depends on.
Now the other side, at its best.
An Advaita teacher answers: the refrain keeps saying that is the self, and names the son right after; the plain flow of the sentence joins that to you.

teach.h: ONE TO LOVE, ONE WHO LOVES.
teach.b: And a Dvaita reader answers back: joined isn't the same; a bird and its post are joined, and still two. Ramanuja's school stands between them, with one Brahman and the self as its body.
All three schools take the Chandogya as scripture.
They part ways on what its three words mean, and each has teachers who argue it with care.

how: In the Dvaita tradition that follows Madhva, the Chandogya is studied with his commentary, which reads the refrain as teaching a real and lasting difference between the self and the Lord, the ground of devotion.

o: that you are, or, for Madhva, you are not that
you are that person, so copy what they do
that self belongs to you, so you can keep it

games.q: three schools, one line. tap the pairs.
p: one Brahman, the self its body

s: Madhva's reading depends on how spoken Sanskrit runs sounds together
where two a-sounds meet they merge, so 'sa atma tat' can also be heard as 'sa atma atat', not that.
Madhva rejected the Chandogya as scripture
all three schools take it as scripture; they part ways on what the line means.

games.q: in a study group you hold the Advaita reading, and you're asked to give Madhva's best case in one line. which is it?
o: a real, lasting difference makes devotion possible: one to love, one who loves.
Madhva simply didn't know Sanskrit well enough to read the line.
for Madhva the difference is a flaw, one to get past in the end.
games.why: for Madhva the self and the Lord are really different, and the difference lasts; the bird and its post, the river and the sea, show dependence.

practice: If there's water nearby, take one slow sip. If you pray, offer it in your heart first, the way many Hindu families offer food and water to God before they take it.
Feel it cool the mouth and go down: something your body needed and didn't make. Rest in that small dependence for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi: one Chandogya line, heard as one awareness, as one Brahman with its body, and, by Madhva, as a real difference.

orig.note: Sanskrit: atat tvam asi, 'you are not that', the Dvaita reading of the seam after sa atma.

carryVoice: Remember this: for Madhva, the difference is what makes devotion possible. Three schools, one line, read with care. Next, a new saying.
